title: each as a lens for a week
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: at the eye doctor's, one lens clicks in after another: "better like this, or like this?" the six darshanas work the same way

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed our visit with Vedanta, revisited: from the Brahma Sutra's first word, now, to its last, no return, said twice. What finished thing did you let stay finished? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.
screen: `VEDANTA: NOW TO NO RETURN.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: You're sitting in the eye doctor's chair, chin on the rest, a heavy metal frame in front of your face. Click. A lens drops in. Better like this? Click. Or like this? The letters on the wall don't change. What changes is how they come to you. Some lenses make the top line sharp and the bottom line a blur. Some do the opposite. Nobody in that chair thinks the lenses are fighting each other. They're tools for seeing. Lately we've walked through the six darshanas, the classical schools of Hindu thought. Today, at the end of a week, we start learning to use them that way: each one as a lens.
screen: `CLICK. BETTER LIKE THIS?` → `THE LETTERS DON'T CHANGE.` → `SIX SCHOOLS, SIX LENSES.`

segments.voice: Start with the word itself. Darshana means a view, a way of seeing. It's the same word Hindus use at the temple, for seeing the deity and being seen. So a school of thought, in this tradition, is named for an act of looking. First, what's behind us. Mimamsa read the ritual act as meaning. Then Vedanta, revisited: a book that opens with the wish to know Brahman, a definition that points like a branch at the moon, one line, you are that, heard three ways, a shared shelf every school writes on, and a last line said twice. Now step back. One way to hold the six schools is by the question each one keeps asking. Nyaya asks: how do I know? Vaisheshika asks: what is this made of? Samkhya asks: who is watching? Yoga asks: what is the mind doing right now? Mimamsa asks: what is this act for? Vedanta asks: what does all of it rest on? Those are our short versions, not the schools' own words. But each one is a real lens. Click one in and certain things go sharp. Over the next few days we'll try them two at a time, on ordinary moments: a rumor, a flash of anger, a sink full of dishes. Then comes the invitation in the title. Each as a lens for a week. Not to choose a winner. This part of the path is called schools of thought, never ranked, and that's the rule we keep.
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `THE WEEK: MIMAMSA AND VEDANTA.` · `SIX SCHOOLS, SIX QUESTIONS.` · `LENSES, NOT RIVALS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the six questions pass through one moment. Settle, and choose something simple, the feeling of sitting where you are. Ask it gently, once each, and don't answer in words. How do I know I'm sitting? What is this made of? Who is noticing it? What is the mind doing? What is this sitting for? What does it rest on? Then let the questions go, and just sit, letting the moment be seen without any lens at all. If you pray, you can offer the moment as it is. The bell holds the time.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, held not as rivals, but as ways of seeing you can try on one at a time. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each as a lens for a week. Today, pick one of the six questions and ask it of the next thing that annoys you. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy traditionally study the six darshanas in pairs, Nyaya with Vaisheshika, Samkhya with Yoga, and Mimamsa with Vedanta, and Hindus also use the word darshana for seeing the deity at a temple.
